title: Functional Dependencies & Normalization
subtitle: Functional dependencies, closures, candidate keys, anomalies, minimal cover and normalization.
source: DBMS Crash Course Part 1 — Modules 1 to 4. Questions are independently crafted from the module concepts and exam-style patterns supplied for Bank SO IT.
instructions: Choose one answer for each question.
Questions are designed for IBPS SO IT, RRB Scale II IT, SBI SO and similar Computer Science/IT examinations.
Review the explanation, important point, exam trap and hint after submission.

questions.question: Given the functional dependency A → B, which statement is correct?

options.text: A and B must both be candidate keys.
A and B must be foreign keys.

questions.explanation: A → B means that the value of A determines a unique value of B. A is the determinant and B is the dependent attribute.
questions.importantPoint: Left side = determinant; right side = dependent.
questions.examTrap: The arrow direction matters.
questions.hint: Read the dependency from left to right.

questions.question: Given F = {A → B, B → C}, which dependency can be inferred using transitivity?
questions.explanation: From A → B and B → C, transitivity gives A → C.
questions.importantPoint: Transitivity: X → Y and Y → Z imply X → Z.
questions.examTrap: Do not reverse a functional dependency.
questions.hint: Follow the chain from A through B to C.

questions.question: For F = {A → B, B → C}, what is A⁺?
questions.explanation: Start with A; A → B adds B, and B → C then adds C. Therefore A⁺ = {A,B,C}.
questions.importantPoint: Attribute closure repeatedly applies applicable FDs until no new attributes can be added.
questions.examTrap: Do not stop after applying only the first dependency.
questions.hint: Start with A and follow every FD whose left side is contained in the closure.

questions.question: For relation R(A,B,C) with F = {A → B, B → C}, which attribute set is a candidate key?
questions.explanation: A⁺ = {A,B,C}, so A determines all attributes and is minimal. B⁺ lacks A, and C⁺ contains only C.
questions.importantPoint: A is a candidate key because its closure contains all attributes.
questions.examTrap: A candidate key must determine the whole relation and be minimal.
questions.hint: Compute closures of the small candidate sets.

questions.question: For F = {AB → C, C → D}, what is (AB)⁺?
questions.explanation: AB initially contains A and B; AB → C adds C, and C → D then adds D. Thus (AB)⁺ = {A,B,C,D}.
questions.importantPoint: Closure can require multiple FD applications.
questions.examTrap: Do not omit attributes already present in the starting set.
questions.hint: Apply AB → C first, then use the newly obtained C.

questions.question: Suppose R(A,B,C) has F = {AB → C}. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A alone is necessarily a candidate key.
B alone is necessarily a candidate key.
AB can be a candidate key if it is minimal and determines all attributes.
C must be a candidate key.

questions.explanation: AB determines C, and AB already contains A and B. If neither A nor B alone determines all attributes, AB is a candidate key.
questions.importantPoint: A composite candidate key can contain more than one attribute.
questions.examTrap: A determinant is not automatically a candidate key; minimality must also be checked.
questions.hint: Check both uniqueness-by-FD and minimality.

questions.question: Which anomaly occurs when deleting the last employee of a department also removes the only stored information about that department?
questions.explanation: This is a deletion anomaly because removing one fact unintentionally removes another independent fact.
questions.importantPoint: Deletion anomaly = loss of unrelated information caused by a deletion.
questions.examTrap: Update anomaly involves inconsistent repeated facts; insertion anomaly involves inability to store a fact independently.
questions.hint: Look for unintended loss of another fact during deletion.

questions.question: A department name is repeated in 100 employee rows. The department name changes, but only 98 rows are updated. Which anomaly is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Repeated department information that becomes inconsistent after an update is an update anomaly.
questions.importantPoint: Update anomaly = repeated fact must be changed consistently in multiple rows.
questions.examTrap: The issue is not that a row cannot be inserted or that data is deleted.
questions.hint: Look for inconsistent copies of the same fact.

questions.question: Which normal form primarily requires atomic attribute values and removes repeating/non-atomic groups?
questions.explanation: First Normal Form requires atomic values and eliminates repeating groups/non-atomic attribute structures.
questions.importantPoint: 1NF → atomic values.
questions.examTrap: 2NF and 3NF address dependency-based issues after 1NF.
questions.hint: Remember the normalization ladder: atomic → partial → transitive → determinant.

questions.question: A relation has a composite candidate key (A,B) and a non-key attribute C with A → C. Which normal form is violated?
questions.explanation: C depends on only part A of the composite candidate key (A,B), which is a partial dependency and violates 2NF.
questions.importantPoint: 2NF removes partial dependency of non-prime attributes on a proper subset of a candidate key.
questions.examTrap: Partial dependency cannot occur with a single-attribute candidate key.
questions.hint: Compare the determinant A with the full composite key AB.

questions.question: A relation is in 2NF and has a dependency A → B where A is non-key and B is non-key. If A is transitively dependent on a candidate key, which normal form is threatened?
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency of a non-key attribute through another non-key determinant violates the usual 3NF condition.
questions.importantPoint: 3NF removes transitive dependency of non-key attributes on candidate keys.
questions.examTrap: 2NF addresses partial dependency, not transitive dependency.
questions.hint: Look for a non-key determinant between the key and another non-key attribute.

questions.question: Which condition is characteristic of BCNF?

options.text: No candidate key may contain more than one attribute.
Every determinant of a non-trivial functional dependency must be a candidate key.
Every relation must have exactly one candidate key.

questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant of every non-trivial functional dependency to be a candidate key.
questions.importantPoint: BCNF → every determinant is a candidate key.
questions.examTrap: BCNF does not require single-attribute keys.
questions.hint: Focus on the left-hand side of every non-trivial FD.

questions.question: Can a partial dependency exist when the only candidate key consists of a single attribute?

options.text: Yes, because every FD is partial.
Yes, if the dependent attribute is non-prime.
No, because there is no proper subset of a single-attribute key.

questions.explanation: A partial dependency requires dependence on a proper subset of a composite candidate key. A single-attribute key has no proper non-empty subset that can form such a partial dependency.
questions.importantPoint: Partial dependency requires a composite candidate key.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse “non-key determinant” with “partial dependency.”
questions.hint: Ask whether a proper subset of the candidate key exists.

questions.question: For F = {A → B, B → C, A → C}, which FD is redundant in a minimal cover?
questions.explanation: A → C is implied by A → B and B → C through transitivity, so it can be removed without changing the closure of the FD set.
questions.importantPoint: A minimal cover removes redundant dependencies.
questions.examTrap: An FD is redundant if it can be derived from the remaining dependencies.
questions.hint: Try deriving A → C without using A → C itself.

questions.question: For F = {AB → C, A → C}, what can be said about the left side of AB → C?

options.text: B is extraneous because A → C already holds.
A is extraneous because B → C is given.
Neither A nor B can ever be extraneous.
AB → C must be removed because it is a candidate key.

questions.explanation: Since A → C already holds, AB → C adds no information beyond A → C; B is extraneous from the left side of AB → C.
questions.importantPoint: Minimal cover removes extraneous attributes from determinants when possible.
questions.examTrap: Do not remove an attribute merely because it appears in a composite determinant; test extraneousness.
questions.hint: Compare AB → C with the existing A → C dependency.

questions.question: For relation R(A,B,C,D) with F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}, which attribute is a candidate key?
questions.explanation: A⁺ = {A,B,C,D}; B⁺ lacks A, C⁺ lacks A and B, and D⁺ contains only D. Thus A is the candidate key.
questions.importantPoint: A candidate key must determine every attribute and be minimal.
questions.examTrap: The chain does not work backward.
questions.hint: Follow the dependency chain starting from each candidate.

questions.question: A relation R(A,B,C) has F = {A → B, B → A, B → C}. Which of the following is a candidate key?
questions.explanation: A⁺ = {A,B,C} through A → B and B → C; B⁺ = {A,B,C} through B → A and B → C. Both A and B are minimal determinants, so both are candidate keys.
questions.importantPoint: A relation can have multiple candidate keys.
questions.examTrap: Do not assume the first determinant found is the only candidate key.
questions.hint: Compute A⁺ and B⁺, then test minimality.

questions.question: A relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF. Which statement can be true?

options.text: Every determinant is a candidate key.
There exists a non-trivial FD whose determinant is not a candidate key, while its dependent attribute is prime.
A partial dependency on a proper subset of a candidate key must exist.

questions.explanation: 3NF can allow certain dependencies where the determinant is not a superkey if the dependent attribute is prime; BCNF would reject such a determinant.
questions.importantPoint: BCNF is stricter than 3NF.
questions.examTrap: Not every 3NF relation is necessarily in BCNF.
questions.hint: Compare the determinant requirement of BCNF with the prime-attribute exception in 3NF.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly represents the usual progression of normalization requirements?
questions.explanation: The standard progression is 1NF, then 2NF, then 3NF, with BCNF being a stronger normal form.
questions.importantPoint: 1NF → atomic; 2NF → no partial dependency; 3NF → no problematic transitive dependency; BCNF → every determinant is a candidate key.
questions.examTrap: Do not place BCNF before 1NF in the normalization ladder.
questions.hint: Recall the order from weaker to stronger requirements.

questions.question: Consider R(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, Grade) with candidate key (StudentID, CourseID) and FD StudentID → StudentName. What is the main normalization issue?

options.text: No issue because StudentName depends on StudentID.
A partial dependency exists because StudentName depends on part of the composite key.
The relation violates only BCNF, not 2NF.

questions.explanation: StudentName depends only on StudentID, which is a proper subset of the composite candidate key, so the relation has a partial dependency and violates 2NF.
questions.importantPoint: Partial dependency is a 2NF violation.
questions.examTrap: The fact that the determinant is meaningful does not make the dependency full.
questions.hint: Compare StudentID with the complete key StudentID + CourseID.
